To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the southern cattle tick R. microplus has a low genetic diversity and a high genetic differentiation in New Caledonia, with the presence of a few highly differentiated populations, which are likely to be the result of the tick's recent introduction to the island, its low dispersal ability and a low number of founders.
the genetic structure of the southern cattle tick is mainly shaped by its high dispersal ability and the absence of barriers to gene flow.

the population genetics of R. microplus on New Caledonia is characterized by (i) a high level of population structuration with a strong genetic differentiation between the northern and southern islands; (ii) a high level genetic structuration within each island; (iii) a strong genetic differentiation of the northern island population into two distinct genetic clusters; (iv) an absence of genetic differentiation between the southern island and the Australian continent; and (v) the absence of genetic differentiation within the southern island population
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: (1) the genetic diversity of the species in its native and invasive ranges; (2) the genetic structure of the invasive populations; (3) the genetic structure and the genetic diversity in relation to environmental variables and (4) the mating system and its relationship to the genetic structure.
the following questions: (i) what are the determinants of the genetic structure of the invasive population?;
the following questions: (1) How does a population of R. microplus invade a new area?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the population genetics of R. microplus in New Caledonia is consistent with the hypothesis that the tick population is structured into two subpopulations, one of which is expanding and the other is stable.
population genetics studies are a powerful tool to investigate tick invasions.
population genetic structure is a complex issue, depending on a large set of ecological and evolutionary processes, which are difficult to disentangle.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(i) the tick population structure is highly structured at the island scale and that the tick genetic diversity is not significantly lower in New Caledonia than in the native continent; (ii) there are two distinct tick lineages, one being more frequent in the northern and the other in the southern parts of the island; (iii) the genetic diversity of the tick population is not correlated to the tick density; and (iv) the tick genetic exchanges seem to be mostly driven by wind-borne
the southern cattle tick is a species with a strong tendency to disperse and to colonize new areas.

the southern cattle tick in New Caledonia is genetically homogeneous, and that the tick populations are likely to be panmictic, but with a strong tendency to local extinction and recolonisation of sites.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sampling design and sampling scales must be adapted to the life cycle of the species, its mating rules, and the geographical scale at which the invasion occurs.

, in order to understand the genetic, demographic and/or ecological processes involved in an invasion, it is necessary to combine a large number of sampling locations, a large sample size, an adequate sampling design (i.e., sampling along a transect) and the analysis of several genetic markers.
population genetics analyses are a useful complement to other biological and ecological approaches to investigate the mechanisms of invasion success.
